'''Gonçalo Rocha Abecasis''' (born 1976) is a [[Portuguese American]] biomedical researcher at the [[University of Michigan]], serves as Vice President & Chief Genomics and Data Science Officer at the Regeneron Genetics Center,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Regn Genetics Center Factsheet (download) |url=https://www.regeneron.com/downloads/regn-genetics-center-factsheet.pdf |website=www.regeneron.com}}</ref> and was chair of the Department of Biostatistics in the [[University of Michigan School of Public Health|School of Public Health]]. He leads a group at the Center for Statistical Genetics in the Department of Biostatistics, where he is also the Felix E. Moore Collegiate Professor of Biostatistics and director of the Michigan Genomic Initiative.<ref name=accolades>{{cite news|url=https://www.michigandaily.com/news/goncalo-abecasis-recognized-top-researcher|title=University professor earns accolades for research on genome sequencing|last=Greenberg|first=Will|date=12 June 2013|work=Michigan Daily|access-date=17 December 2013}}</ref> His group develops statistical tools to analyze the [[Medical genetics|genetics of human disease]].<ref>{{Google Scholar id |name=Goncalo Abecasis}}<br> {{Scopus |name= Abecasis, Gonçalo R.}}<br>- {{DBLP |name=Gonçalo R. ==Education and early life==
Abecasis is the oldest of 12 children in his family, born in [[Moura Municipality|Moura]] to José Manuel and Maria Teresa.<ref name="geneall">{{cite web
 |url=http://www.geneall.net/P/per_page.php?id=507681
 |title=Gonçalo Rocha Abecasis
 |year=2014
 |publisher=Geneall.net
 |archive-date=2014-01-08
 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140108010059/http://www.geneall.net/P/per_page.php?id=507681
 |url-status=dead
}}</ref> He grew up in [[Portugal]] and [[Macau]] (then [[Portuguese Macau]]). After learning computer programming in a high school club, he received a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree in Genetics from the [[University of Leeds]] in 1997, working with Marie-Anne Shaw, and a [[Doctor of Philosophy|D. Phil]] in [[human genetics]]<ref name="abecasisphd">{{cite thesis |degree=DPhil |first=Gonçalo|last=Abecasis |title=Methods for fine mapping complex traits in human pedigrees |publisher=University of Oxford |date=2002 |url=http://solo.bodleian.ox.ac.uk/primo_library/libweb/action/dlDisplay.do?docId=oxfaleph015401584|author-link=Gonçalo Abecasis}}</ref> from the [[University of Oxford]] in 2001, working with William Cookson  and [[Lon Cardon]].<ref name=spectrum/><ref name=congrats>{{cite web|url=https://www.iscb.org/iscb-awards/1837|title=Congratulations to 2013 ISCB Overton Prize Winner: Goncalo Abecasis|last=Fogg|first=Christine N.|date=28 June 2013|work=ISCB|access-date=17 December 2013}}</ref>

==Research==
Abecasis works on statistical and computational approaches to human genetic disease, including psoriasis and cardiovascular diseases.<ref name=spectrum>{{cite web|url=https://spectrum.ieee.org/profile-goncalo-abecasis-mines-gnomes-for-biomedical-gold|title=Profile: Gonçalo Abecasis Mines Genomes for Biomedical Gold|last=Karlin|first=Susan|date=17 September 2013|work=IEEE Spectrum|access-date=17 December 2013}}</ref> His group develops tools to analyze and visualize biomedical data, often using [[C++]].<ref name=spectrum/> He first applied his programming knowledge during his Ph.D. studies to develop tools to analyze the data on asthma susceptibility that his project was generating. He continued as a biostatistician when he moved to Michigan in 2001, where he was recruited and mentored by [[Michael Boehnke]].<ref name="overton"/><ref name=spectrum/><ref name=congrats/> He is a proponent of [[data sharing]].<ref name=congrats/> His work has included the [[1000 Genomes Project]]<ref name="1000genomes">{{Cite journal | last1 = Durbin | first1 = R. ==Awards and honours==
Abecasis won an Excellence in Research Award from the University of Michigan School of Public Health in 2008,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.sph.umich.edu/about/awards.html |title=Faculty Awards for Excellence |work=University of Michigan School of Public Health |access-date=17 December 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140108005129/http://www.sph.umich.edu/about/awards.html |archive-date=8 January 2014 }}</ref> and he became a professor at the University of Michigan in 2009.<ref name=spectrum/> He won the 2013 [[Overton Prize]] from the International Society for Computational Biology, giving a [[List of Intelligent Systems for Molecular Biology keynote speakers|keynote speech at the ISMB]],<ref name="overton"/> and was named a [[Pew Scholar]] by the Pew Charitable Trusts in 2005.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://directory.pewscholars.org/scholars/2005-115/ |archive-url=https://archive.today/20140304102718/http://directory.pewscholars.org/scholars/2005-115/ |url-status=dead |archive-date=2014-03-04 |title=Pew Scholars Directory |work=Pew Charitable Trusts Website |access-date=2014-03-04}}</ref> His work was cited in 2010 by US Vice-President [[Joe Biden]] in a speech on the importance of biomedical research regarding the Recovery Act Innovation Report.<ref name=congrats/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ur.umich.edu/update/archives/100825/research|title=Biden: U-M transforming economy through innovation|last=Serwach|first=Joe|date=25 August 2010|work=University of Michigan News Service|access-date=17 December 2013}}</ref>

His published work is influential - as of 2018, he had an [[h-index]] of 145 and 144,018 citations. [[Thomson Reuters]] noted that he had 10 'hot papers' (in the top 0.1% by citations) in 2009.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://archive.sciencewatch.com/ana/fea/10maraprFea/|title=The Hottest Research of 2009|last=King|first=Christopher|date=March–April 2010|work=Sciencewatch.com|publisher=Thomson Reuters|access-date=17 December 2013}}</ref> He was also noted for his 'hot papers' in 2011 and 2012.<ref name=accolades/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://sciencewatch.com/articles/hottest-research-2012|title=The Hottest Scientific Researchers of 2012|date=June 2013|work=Science Watch|publisher=Thomson Reuters|access-date=17 December 2013}}<br>- {{cite web|url=http://sciencewatch.com/articles/hottest-research-2011|title=The Hottest Research of 2011|last=King|first=Christopher|date=September 2012|work=Sciencewatch.com|publisher=Thomson Reuters|access-date=17 December 2013}}</ref>

In October 2014, he was awarded the [[Curt Stern Award]] in Human Genetics by the [[American Society of Human Genetics]] (jointly with [[Mark J. Daly]]).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ashg.org/pages/awards_pastrecipients.shtml#stern|title=Past Award Recipients|date=October 2014|work=ashg.org|publisher=American Society of Human Genetics|access-date=17 October 2014|archive-date=3 October 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141003163707/http://www.ashg.org/pages/awards_pastrecipients.shtml#stern|url-status=dead}}</ref>

He was elected to the [[Institute of Medicine]] in October 2014.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www8.nationalacademies.org/onpinews/newsitem.aspx?RecordID=10202014A | title=Institute Of Medicine Elects 70 New Members, 10 Foreign Associates | work=National Academy of Sciences | date=20 October 2014 | access-date=22 October 2014}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Goncalo is married to University of Michigan scientist [[Cristen Willer]]. They have five children.<ref name=geneall/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.sph.umich.edu/csg/abecasis/photos/index.html|title=Gonçalo and Cristen's Picture Album|work=Gonçalo Abecasis|publisher=University of Michigan|access-date=17 December 2013}}<br>- {{cite web|url=http://www.hg.med.umich.edu/faculty/cristen-willer-phd|title=Cristen Willer Faculty Profile|work=University of Michigan Medical School Faculty|publisher=University of Michigan|access-date=8 February 2014}}</ref>
